Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 78, verses 1–5:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿About what do they ask one another? About the great news, about which they are in disagreement. No! They are going to know. Then, no! They are going to know.﴾

Exalted is He, says: About what do these polytheists among the Quraysh, who associate others with Allah and with His Messenger, ask one another, O Muhammad? It is said that this was addressed to him (ﷺ), because the Quraysh, as is reported about them, were disputing and arguing about what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had called them to: acknowledging his prophethood, believing in what he brought from Allah, and having faith in the Resurrection. So Allah said to His Prophet: About what do these people ask one another and dispute? The "fi" (in) and the " 'an" (about) in this context have the same meaning.

Mention of those who said this:

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' ibn al-Jarrah narrated to us, from Mis'ar, from Muhammad ibn Juhadah, from al-Hasan, who said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent, they began to ask one another, so Allah revealed: ﴿About what do they ask one another? About the great news﴾, meaning: the great report.

Abu Ja'far said: Then Allah informed His Prophet (ﷺ) about what they were asking one another, saying: They ask one another about the great news, meaning: about the great report.

The people of interpretation differed concerning what is meant by "the great news." Some of them said: It refers to the Qur'an.

Mention of those who said this:

Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the words of Allah: ﴿About the great news﴾, he said: The Qur'an.

Others said: It refers to the Resurrection.

Mention of those who said this:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿About the great news﴾, which is the resurrection after death.

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Sa'id, from Qatadah: ﴿About the great news﴾, he said: The great news is the resurrection after death.

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: ﴿About what do they ask one another? About the great news about which they are in disagreement﴾, he said: It is the Day of Resurrection. He said: They said, "This is the day you claim we and our fathers will be brought to life in," and so they are in disagreement about it, not believing in it. Then Allah said: Rather, it is a great news from which you turn away: the Day of Resurrection, which they do not believe in.

Some of the scholars of Arabic grammar used to say: The meaning of that is: "About what do the Quraysh speak concerning the Qur'an?" Then He answered, so "'amma" became as if it meant: "About what do they ask one another concerning the Qur'an?" Then He informed, saying: ﴿about which they are in disagreement﴾, between one who confirms and one who denies. That is their disagreement. His saying ﴿about which they are in disagreement﴾ means, exalted is He: about which they have become divided into two groups: a group that confirms it and a group that denies it. Exalted is He says: So their questioning among themselves is about news of this description.

The people of interpretation said things similar to what we have said.

Mention of those who said this:

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah: "about the news ﴿about which they are in disagreement﴾": the resurrection after death, so people became two groups concerning it: one who confirms and one who denies. As for death, they acknowledged it, because they witnessed it, but they disagreed about resurrection after death.

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: ﴿about which they are in disagreement﴾, people became two men concerning it: one who confirms and one who denies. As for death, they all acknowledged it, because they witnessed it, but they disagreed about resurrection after death.

Ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah: ﴿about which they are in disagreement﴾, he said: one who confirms and one who denies.

His saying: ﴿No!﴾

Exalted is He says: The matter is not as these polytheists claim, those who deny that Allah will resurrect them alive after their death. He threatened them for this statement of theirs, saying: ﴿They are going to know﴾, meaning: these deniers, the enemies of Allah, will know the threat of Allah, what Allah will do to them on the Day of Resurrection. Then He emphasized the threat with another repetition, saying: The matter is not as they claim, that Allah will not bring them back to life after their death, nor punish them for their disbelief in Him. They will know that the statement is other than what they said when they meet Allah and arrive at what they sent ahead of their evil deeds.

It is reported from al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim regarding this:

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Abu Sinan, from Thabit, from al-Dahhak: ﴿No! They are going to know﴾ refers to the disbelievers, ﴿Then, no! They are going to know﴾ refers to the believers. And so he used to recite it.

The Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 78, verses 6–11:

The explanation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have We not made the earth a cradle (mihad),﴾ ﴿and the mountains as pegs?﴾ ﴿And We created you in pairs,﴾ ﴿and made your sleep a rest,﴾ ﴿and made the night a covering,﴾ ﴿and made the day for livelihood.﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says, enumerating to these polytheists His blessings and favours upon them, His kindness toward them, and their ingratitude for what He has bestowed upon them, and threatening them with the various kinds of His punishment and the painful torment He has prepared for them when they come before Him, so He said to them: ﴿Have We not made the earth﴾ for you ﴿a cradle (mihad)﴾, which you spread out and lay down upon.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 78, verse 12–14:

The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We built above you seven strong [heavens]﴾ (12) ﴿and We made a blazing lamp﴾ (13) ﴿and sent down from the rain-clouds abundant water﴾ (14).

His saying, may His remembrance be exalted: ﴿And We built above you﴾: We roofed over you. He called the roof a building because the Arabs used to call the ceilings of houses, which are their sky, a building (bina'), and the sky was the roof of the earth. So He addressed them in their own language, since the revelation was in their language. He said ﴿seven strong﴾ because they are firmly created structures, with no cracks or fissures in them, and the passing of nights and days does not wear them out.

* *

And His saying: ﴿And We made a blazing lamp﴾

His saying, may His remembrance be exalted: "And We made a lamp," by the lamp He means the sun. His saying ﴿blazing﴾ means: a burning, shining flame.

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) said the same as what we have said on this matter.

Mention of those who said that:

- Ali related to me, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiya related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And We made a blazing lamp﴾ — he said: shining.

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿And We made a blazing lamp﴾ — he said: a lamp giving light.

- Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa related to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿a lamp blazing﴾ — he said: it gleams.

- Ibn Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada: ﴿a blazing lamp﴾ — he said: al-wahhaj: the shining.

- Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Mihran related to us, from Sufyan: ﴿a blazing lamp﴾ — he said: its light gleams.

* *

And His saying: ﴿And sent down from the rain-clouds﴾

The people of interpretation differed concerning what is meant by al-mu'sirat (the rain-clouds). Some of them said: what is meant by them is the winds that squeeze (ta'sir) as they blow.

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And sent down from the rain-clouds﴾ — al-mu'sirat: the wind.

- Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Yahya ibn Wadih related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, from Yazid, from Ikrima, that he used to recite ﴿wa-anzalna bil-mu'sirat﴾, meaning: the winds.

- Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿from the rain-clouds﴾ — he said: the wind.

- And al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the same.

- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada, who said: in some readings it is ﴿wa-anzalna bil-mu'sirat﴾: the winds.

- Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: ﴿And sent down from the rain-clouds﴾: al-mu'sirat are the winds, and he recited the saying of God: "It is God who sends the winds, and they stir up clouds..." to the end of the verse.

Others said: rather, they are the clouds that are dripping with rain but have not yet rained, like the young woman (al-mu'sir) who is close to the time of her menstruation but has not yet menstruated.

Mention of those who said that:

- Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Mihran related to us, from Sufyan: ﴿from the rain-clouds﴾ — he said: al-mu'sirat: the clouds.

- Ali related to me, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiya related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And sent down from the rain-clouds﴾ — he said: from the clouds.

- He said: Mihran related to us, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Rabi': ﴿al-mu'sirat﴾: the clouds.

Others said: rather, it is the sky.

Mention of those who said that:

- Ya'qub related to me, saying: Ibn Ulayya related to us, from Abu Raja', who said: I heard al-Hasan say: ﴿And sent down from the rain-clouds﴾ — he said: from the sky.

- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada, regarding His saying: ﴿And sent down from the rain-clouds﴾ — he said: from the heavens.

- Ibn Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada, regarding His saying: ﴿And sent down from the rain-clouds﴾ — he said: from the sky.

The most correct of these opinions is to say: God informs that He sent down water from al-mu'sirat, which are the clouds that have dripped with water.

We say this is the more correct view because, on any of the three opinions mentioned, the matter would be that water is sent down from them; but the winds contain no water that would be sent down from them, rather rain is sent down by them. And had the reading been ﴿wa-anzalna bil-mu'sirat﴾ it would have been possible for it to be the winds. But since the reading is ﴿min al-mu'sirat﴾, it is known that what is meant is what I have described.

If someone supposes that the preposition ba' (bi-) may follow in such a context with the same meaning, even if that is so, the more usual meaning of min is otherwise, and interpretation follows the more usual meaning of speech. If he says: the sky may also be intended, it is said: even if that is so, the more usual source of rain is the clouds rather than anything else.

As for His saying: ﴿abundant water﴾ (ma'an thajjajan), He means: water poured forth, following one another, like the pouring of the blood of sacrificial camels, which is its shedding.

The people of interpretation said the same as what we have said on this matter.

Mention of those who said that:

- Ali related to me, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiya related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿abundant water﴾ — he said: poured forth.

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿abundant water﴾ — water from the sky, poured forth.

- Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa related to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿abundant water﴾ — he said: poured forth.

- Ibn Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada: ﴿abundant water﴾ — he said: al-thajjaj: the poured forth.

- Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Mihran related to us, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Rabi': ﴿abundant water﴾ — he said: poured forth.

- He said: Mihran related to us, from Sufyan: ﴿abundant water﴾ — he said: following one another.

Some of them said: what is meant by al-thajjaj is: abundant.

Mention of those who said that:

- Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us: ﴿abundant water﴾ — he said: plentiful. But thajj is not known in the speech of the Arabs as a description of abundance; rather, thajj is pouring that follows continuously. Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 78, verse 15–20:

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿That We may bring forth thereby grain and vegetation, and gardens of entwined growth.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the Day of Judgement is a appointed time,﴾ ﴿the Day the Horn is blown and you come forth in multitudes,﴾ ﴿and the sky is opened and becomes gateways,﴾ ﴿and the mountains are set in motion and become a mirage.﴾

His words, may He be remembered: "That We may bring forth thereby grain" by the water We send down from the rain-laden clouds to the earth. Grain (ḥabb) is everything contained within the husks of the crops that are harvested; it is the plural of ḥabbah, just as shaʿīr (barley) is the plural of shaʿīrah, and tamr (dates) is the plural of tamrah. As for "vegetation" (nabāt), it is the pasture that is grazed, consisting of grass and crops.

* *

His words: ﴿and gardens of entwined growth﴾

He says: And We bring forth by that rain gardens (jannāt), which are orchards. He said "gardens" (jannāt), and the meaning is "and the fruit of gardens," so the mention of the fruit is omitted, as the context indicates it.

* *

His words: ﴿entwined growth (alfāfan)﴾

That is: intertwined and gathered together.

The exegetes have said what is similar to what we have said.

Those who said that:

⁕ ʿAlī narrated to me: Abū Ṣāliḥ narrated to us, saying: Muʿāwiyah narrated to me, from ʿAlī, from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His words: ﴿and gardens of entwined growth﴾, he said: gathered together.

⁕ Muḥammad ibn Saʿd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbās, ﴿and gardens of entwined growth﴾, he says: gardens whose parts are intertwined with one another.

⁕ Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abū ʿĀṣim narrated to us, saying: ʿĪsā narrated to us, and al-Ḥārith narrated to me, saying: al-Ḥasan narrated to us, saying: Warqāʾ narrated to us, all from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, ﴿and gardens of entwined growth﴾, he said: intertwined.

⁕ Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazīd narrated to us, saying: Saʿīd narrated to us, from Qatādah, regarding His words: ﴿and gardens of entwined growth﴾, he said: some of them intertwined with others.

⁕ Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Maʿmar, from Qatādah, regarding His words: ﴿and gardens of entwined growth﴾, he said: some of them intertwined with others.

⁕ Ibn Ḥumayd narrated to us, saying: Mihrān narrated to us, from Sufyān: ﴿and gardens of entwined growth﴾, he said: intertwined.

⁕ Yūnus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words: ﴿and gardens of entwined growth﴾, he said: they are the intertwined ones, some above others.

The grammarians of Arabic differed concerning the singular of alfāf. Some of the grammarians of Basra said: its singular is laff. Some of the grammarians of Kufa said: its singular is laff and lafīf. He said: If you wish, alfāf can be a plural whose singular is also a plural, so you say: jannah laffāʾ (a dense garden), and jannāt laff, then laff is pluralised as alfāf.

Another of them said: We have not heard shajarah laffah; rather its singular is laffāʾ and its plural is laff, and the plural of laff is alfāf, so it is a plural of a plural.

The correct view on this is that alfāf is the plural of laff or lafīf. This is because the exegetes agree that its meaning is "intertwined," and laffāʾ means "thick," and intertwining has nothing to do with thickness, unless it is taken to mean the thickness of the intertwining, in which case that would be a valid interpretation.

* *

His words: ﴿Indeed, the Day of Judgement is an appointed time﴾

He, may He be remembered, says: Indeed, the Day on which God separates His creatures, judging among them and taking from some of them for others, was an appointed time for what God had decreed for those who denied the resurrection and for their companions among creation.

The exegetes have said what is similar to what we have said.

Those who said that:

⁕ Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazīd narrated to us, saying: Saʿīd narrated to us, from Qatādah, regarding His words: ﴿Indeed, the Day of Judgement is an appointed time﴾, he said: it is a Day which God magnified, on which God separates the first and the last according to their deeds.

* *

His words: ﴿the Day the Horn is blown﴾

He rendered "the Day the Horn is blown" as an explanation of "the Day of Judgement," as if it were said: The Day of Judgement is the term that was promised to these people: the Day the Horn is blown. The meaning of the Ṣūr (Horn) has already been explained earlier, and the differences of the exegetes concerning it have been mentioned, so there is no need to repeat it here. It is, in our view, a horn into which one blows.

As related:

⁕ Ibn Ḥumayd narrated to us, saying: Mihrān narrated to us, from Sufyān, from Sulaymān al-Taymī, from Aslam, from Bishr ibn Shaghāf, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The Ṣūr is a horn."

⁕ Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazīd narrated to us, saying: Saʿīd narrated to us, from Qatādah, regarding His words: ﴿the Day the Horn is blown﴾, he said: the Ṣūr is the creation.

* *

His words: ﴿and you come forth in multitudes﴾

He says: They will come in groups, company after company.

The exegetes have said what is similar to what we have said.

Those who said that:

⁕ Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to us, saying: Abū ʿĀṣim narrated to us, saying: ʿĪsā narrated to us, and al-Ḥārith narrated to me, saying: al-Ḥasan narrated to us, saying: Warqāʾ narrated to us, all from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, regarding His words: ﴿in multitudes﴾, he said: in groups, group after group.

It is only said: ﴿and you come forth in multitudes﴾ because every nation to which God sent a messenger comes with the one who was sent to it, as He said: ﴿The Day We shall call every people with their leader﴾.

His words: ﴿and the sky is opened and becomes gateways﴾

He, may He be remembered, says: The sky is split and cleft, and becomes paths. Previously it was solid, with no cracks or fissures in it. It has also been said that the meaning is: the sky is opened and becomes pieces, like pieces of split wood for the doors of houses and dwellings. They said: the meaning of the sentence is: the sky is opened and becomes pieces like doors, and when the particle "ka" (like) is dropped, "the doors" becomes the predicate, as one says in speech: "ʿAbd Allāh was a lion," meaning: like a lion.

* *

His words: ﴿and the mountains are set in motion and become a mirage﴾

He says: The mountains are uprooted and pulled from their foundations, and made into scattered dust, visible to the eye of the beholder, like a mirage which one who sees it from afar supposes to be water, while in reality it is dust.

It is only said: ﴿and you come forth in multitudes﴾ because every nation to which God sent a messenger comes with the one who was sent to it, as He said: ﴿The Day We shall call every people with their leader﴾.

His words: ﴿and the sky is opened and becomes gateways﴾

He, may He be remembered, says: The sky is split and cleft, and becomes paths. Previously it was solid, with no cracks or fissures in it. It has also been said that the meaning is: the sky is opened and becomes pieces, like pieces of split wood for the doors of houses and dwellings. They said: the meaning of the sentence is: the sky is opened and becomes pieces like doors, and when the particle "ka" (like) is dropped, "the doors" becomes the predicate, as one says in speech: "ʿAbd Allāh was a lion," meaning: like a lion.

* *

His words: ﴿and the mountains are set in motion and become a mirage﴾

He says: The mountains are uprooted and pulled from their foundations, and made into scattered dust, visible to the eye of the beholder, like a mirage which one who sees it from afar supposes to be water, while in reality it is dust.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 78, verse 15–20:

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿That We may bring forth thereby grain and vegetation, and gardens of entwined growth.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the Day of Judgement is a appointed time,﴾ ﴿the Day the Horn is blown and you come forth in multitudes,﴾ ﴿and the sky is opened and becomes gateways,﴾ ﴿and the mountains are set in motion and become a mirage.﴾

His words, may He be remembered: "That We may bring forth thereby grain" by the water We send down from the rain-laden clouds to the earth. Grain (ḥabb) is everything contained within the husks of the crops that are harvested; it is the plural of ḥabbah, just as shaʿīr (barley) is the plural of shaʿīrah, and tamr (dates) is the plural of tamrah. As for "vegetation" (nabāt), it is the pasture that is grazed, consisting of grass and crops.

* *

His words: ﴿and gardens of entwined growth﴾

He says: And We bring forth by that rain gardens (jannāt), which are orchards. He said "gardens" (jannāt), and the meaning is "and the fruit of gardens," so the mention of the fruit is omitted, as the context indicates it.

* *

His words: ﴿entwined growth (alfāfan)﴾

That is: intertwined and gathered together.

The exegetes have said what is similar to what we have said.

Those who said that:

⁕ ʿAlī narrated to me: Abū Ṣāliḥ narrated to us, saying: Muʿāwiyah narrated to me, from ʿAlī, from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His words: ﴿and gardens of entwined growth﴾, he said: gathered together.

⁕ Muḥammad ibn Saʿd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbās, ﴿and gardens of entwined growth﴾, he says: gardens whose parts are intertwined with one another.

⁕ Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abū ʿĀṣim narrated to us, saying: ʿĪsā narrated to us, and al-Ḥārith narrated to me, saying: al-Ḥasan narrated to us, saying: Warqāʾ narrated to us, all from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, ﴿and gardens of entwined growth﴾, he said: intertwined.

⁕ Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazīd narrated to us, saying: Saʿīd narrated to us, from Qatādah, regarding His words: ﴿and gardens of entwined growth﴾, he said: some of them intertwined with others.

⁕ Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Maʿmar, from Qatādah, regarding His words: ﴿and gardens of entwined growth﴾, he said: some of them intertwined with others.

⁕ Ibn Ḥumayd narrated to us, saying: Mihrān narrated to us, from Sufyān: ﴿and gardens of entwined growth﴾, he said: intertwined.

⁕ Yūnus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words: ﴿and gardens of entwined growth﴾, he said: they are the intertwined ones, some above others.

The grammarians of Arabic differed concerning the singular of alfāf. Some of the grammarians of Basra said: its singular is laff. Some of the grammarians of Kufa said: its singular is laff and lafīf. He said: If you wish, alfāf can be a plural whose singular is also a plural, so you say: jannah laffāʾ (a dense garden), and jannāt laff, then laff is pluralised as alfāf.

Another of them said: We have not heard shajarah laffah; rather its singular is laffāʾ and its plural is laff, and the plural of laff is alfāf, so it is a plural of a plural.

The correct view on this is that alfāf is the plural of laff or lafīf. This is because the exegetes agree that its meaning is "intertwined," and laffāʾ means "thick," and intertwining has nothing to do with thickness, unless it is taken to mean the thickness of the intertwining, in which case that would be a valid interpretation.

* *

His words: ﴿Indeed, the Day of Judgement is an appointed time﴾

He, may He be remembered, says: Indeed, the Day on which God separates His creatures, judging among them and taking from some of them for others, was an appointed time for what God had decreed for those who denied the resurrection and for their companions among creation.

The exegetes have said what is similar to what we have said.

Those who said that:

⁕ Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazīd narrated to us, saying: Saʿīd narrated to us, from Qatādah, regarding His words: ﴿Indeed, the Day of Judgement is an appointed time﴾, he said: it is a Day which God magnified, on which God separates the first and the last according to their deeds.

* *

His words: ﴿the Day the Horn is blown﴾

He rendered "the Day the Horn is blown" as an explanation of "the Day of Judgement," as if it were said: The Day of Judgement is the term that was promised to these people: the Day the Horn is blown. The meaning of the Ṣūr (Horn) has already been explained earlier, and the differences of the exegetes concerning it have been mentioned, so there is no need to repeat it here. It is, in our view, a horn into which one blows.

As related:

⁕ Ibn Ḥumayd narrated to us, saying: Mihrān narrated to us, from Sufyān, from Sulaymān al-Taymī, from Aslam, from Bishr ibn Shaghāf, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The Ṣūr is a horn."

⁕ Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazīd narrated to us, saying: Saʿīd narrated to us, from Qatādah, regarding His words: ﴿the Day the Horn is blown﴾, he said: the Ṣūr is the creation.

* *

His words: ﴿and you come forth in multitudes﴾

He says: They will come in groups, company after company.

The exegetes have said what is similar to what we have said.

Those who said that:

⁕ Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to us, saying: Abū ʿĀṣim narrated to us, saying: ʿĪsā narrated to us, and al-Ḥārith narrated to me, saying: al-Ḥasan narrated to us, saying: Warqāʾ narrated to us, all from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, regarding His words: ﴿in multitudes﴾, he said: in groups, group after group.

It is only said: ﴿and you come forth in multitudes﴾ because every nation to which God sent a messenger comes with the one who was sent to it, as He said: ﴿The Day We shall call every people with their leader﴾.

His words: ﴿and the sky is opened and becomes gateways﴾

He, may He be remembered, says: The sky is split and cleft, and becomes paths. Previously it was solid, with no cracks or fissures in it. It has also been said that the meaning is: the sky is opened and becomes pieces, like pieces of split wood for the doors of houses and dwellings. They said: the meaning of the sentence is: the sky is opened and becomes pieces like doors, and when the particle "ka" (like) is dropped, "the doors" becomes the predicate, as one says in speech: "ʿAbd Allāh was a lion," meaning: like a lion.

* *

His words: ﴿and the mountains are set in motion and become a mirage﴾

He says: The mountains are uprooted and pulled from their foundations, and made into scattered dust, visible to the eye of the beholder, like a mirage which one who sees it from afar supposes to be water, while in reality it is dust.

The commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 78, verses 21–25:

﴿Indeed, Hell has been ever lying in wait﴾ ﴿for the transgressors, a place of return,﴾ ﴿remaining therein for ages.﴾ ﴿They will not taste therein any coolness or drink,﴾ ﴿except scalding water and dark, cold liquid.﴾

Concerning the interpretation of His saying: ﴿Indeed, Hell has been ever lying in wait﴾

By His saying, may His remembrance be exalted, He means: Indeed, Hell has been a place of watching for its people, those who used to deny in the world both it and the return to God in the Hereafter, and also for others among those who affirm it. The meaning of the statement is: Indeed, Hell has been a place of lying in wait, watching for whoever passes through it and keeping an eye on them.

The exegetes (ahl al-ta'wil) have said the same as what we have said about this.

Mention of those who said that:

Zakariyya ibn Yahya ibn Abi Za'ida narrated to us, saying: Muslim ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, from Abd Allah ibn Bakr ibn Abd Allah al-Muzani, who said: Al-Hasan, whenever he recited this verse, ﴿Indeed, Hell has been ever lying in wait﴾, would say: "Indeed, at the gate there is a watchman. Whoever comes with a pass will pass through, and whoever does not come with a pass will be detained."

Ya'qub narrated to me, saying: Isma'il ibn Ulayya narrated to us, from Abu Raja', from al-Hasan, regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, Hell has been ever lying in wait﴾, he said: "No one enters Paradise until he passes through the Fire."

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, Hell has been ever lying in wait﴾, he said: "It informs us that there is no path to Paradise until one crosses the Fire."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan: ﴿Indeed, Hell has been ever lying in wait﴾, he said: "On it are three bridges."

* *

As for His saying: ﴿for the transgressors, a place of return﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Indeed, Hell is, for those who transgressed in the world, who exceeded the limits of God out of arrogance toward their Lord, a dwelling and a place of return, to which they return, and a destination to which they go, to dwell in it.

The exegetes have said the same as what we have said about this.

Mention of those who said that:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada: ﴿a place of return﴾, meaning a dwelling and a refuge.

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan: ﴿a place of return﴾, he said: "A place of return and a dwelling."

* *

As for His saying: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Indeed, these transgressors in the world will remain in Hell, abiding therein for ages.

The readers (qurra') differed in the recitation of His saying: ﴿labithin﴾. The majority of the readers of Medina and Basra, and some readers of Kufa, recited it as ﴿labithin﴾ with an alif (lābithīn). The majority of the readers of Kufa recited it as "labithin" without an alif (labithīn). The more eloquent of the two readings, and the one more sound in its grammatical derivation in Arabic, is the reading of the one who recites it with the alif. This is because the Arabs hardly ever use an adjective of the pattern fa'il (ʿafila) and then make it govern something and put it in the accusative by it. They would not say: "This is a man stingy (bakhil) with his wealth," nor "it was difficult (asir) for us," nor "he is a quarrelsome opponent (khasim) to us," because such a pattern as fa'ila does not come as an adjective except to praise or blame, so the praise or blame does not govern anything other than itself. When they want to make such a word govern a noun or something else, they make it an active participle (fā'il) and say: "He is bakhil with his wealth" (bākhil bi-mālihi), and "he is ṭāmi' in what is with us" (ṭāmi' fīmā 'indanā). Therefore I said that lābithīn is more sound in its grammatical derivation in Arabic and more eloquent. I have not deemed lawful the reading of the one who recites labithin, although the other is more eloquent, because the Arabs sometimes make praise govern nouns. A verse of Labid is recited:

"Or a mislah ʿamil, a flank of a smooth-skinned she-ass (samaḥj), with its shoulders having wounds and sores."

So ʿamil governed ʿiḍāda (flank), and if it were an active participle it would have been more eloquent. It is also recited:

"... ... ... ... ... ... ... ... ... and with the axe, a striker of the heads of the karanif (thistle/hard-headed)."

And from it is the saying of ʿAbbās ibn Mirdas:

"More fearless and more protective of the truth than them, and striking with swords the helmets (qawānis) more than us."

As for al-aḥqāb (ages), it is the plural of ḥuqb, and ḥiqab is the plural of ḥiqba, as the poet said:

"We lived like the two companions of Jadhima for an age (ḥiqba) of time, until it was said: we shall not separate."

So this is plural ḥiqab, and among the uses of aḥqāb whose plural is ḥuqb is God's saying: ﴿or I will continue for a long age (ḥuqb)﴾. So this is the singular of aḥqāb.

The exegetes differed concerning the duration of a ḥuqb. Some of them said: it is a duration of three hundred years.

Mention of those who said that:

ʿImran ibn Musa al-Qazzaz narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Warith ibn Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Ishaq ibn Suwayd narrated to us, from Bashir ibn Ka'b, regarding His saying: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾, he said: "It has reached me that a ḥuqb is three hundred years, each year three hundred and sixty days, each day a thousand years."

Others said: rather, the duration of one ḥuqb is eighty years.

Mention of those who said that:

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, who said: ʿAmmar al-Duhni narrated to me, from Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd, who said: ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, said to Hilal al-Hajari: "What do you find of the ḥuqb in the revealed Book of God?" He said: "We find eighty years, each year twelve months, each month thirty days, each day a thousand years."

Tamim ibn al-Muntasir narrated to us, saying: Ishaq informed us, from Shurayk, from ʿAsim ibn Abi al-Najud, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayra, that he said: "The ḥuqb is eighty years, the year is three hundred and sixty days, and the day is a thousand years."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Abu Sinan, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The ḥuqb is eighty years."

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Jabir ibn Nuh narrated to us, saying: al-Aʿmash narrated to us, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, regarding His saying: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾, he said: "The ḥuqb is eighty years, the year is three hundred and sixty days, the day is a year or a thousand years" [al-Tabari is doubtful].

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatada, who said: God said: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾, and it is that which has no end; whenever one ḥuqb passes, another ḥuqb comes after it. It was mentioned to us that the ḥuqb is eighty years.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿla narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Maʿmar, from Qatada, regarding His saying: ﴿aḥqāban﴾, he said: "It has reached us that the ḥuqb is eighty years of the years of the Hereafter."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Abu Jaʿfar, from al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾, "No one knows the number of these ages except God, but one ḥuqb is eighty years, the year is three hundred and sixty days, and each day of that is a thousand years."

Others said: One ḥuqb is seventy thousand years.

Mention of those who said that:

Ibn ʿAbd al-Rahim al-Barqi narrated to me, saying: ʿAmr ibn Abi Salama narrated to me, from Zuhayr, from Salim, who said: I heard al-Hasan being asked about God's saying: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾, and he said: "As for the ages, there is no count of them except eternity in the Fire; but they mentioned that one ḥuqb is seventy thousand years, each day of those seventy thousand days being like a thousand years of what you count."

ʿAmr ibn ʿAbd al-Hamid al-Amuli narrated to us, saying: Abu Usama narrated to us, from Hisham, from al-Hasan, regarding His saying: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾, he said: "As for the ages, no one knows what they are, but one ḥuqb is seventy thousand years, each day like a thousand years."

It is narrated from Khalid ibn Maʿdan regarding this verse that it refers to the people of the qibla (Muslims).

Mention of those who said that:

ʿAli narrated to us, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Muʿawiya ibn Salih narrated to me, from ʿAmir ibn Jashb, from Khalid ibn Maʿdan, regarding His saying: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾, and His saying: ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, that both refer to the people of monotheism from among the people of the qibla.

If someone says: What do you say about this report? It is said: What Qatada said from al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas about this is more sound. If he says: "Then for the disbelievers there is no punishment except ages," it is said: Indeed al-Rabiʿ and Qatada both said that these ages have no end and no cessation. It may also be that the meaning of it is: remaining therein for ages in this type of punishment, and that they: ﴿will not taste therein any coolness or drink, except scalding water and dark, cold liquid﴾. Then when those ages are over, they will have other kinds of punishment beyond that, as God, may His praise be exalted, said in His Book: ﴿And indeed for the transgressors is an evil place of return: Hell, which they will burn in, and wretched is the resting place. This—so let them taste it: scalding water and dark, cold liquid, and other punishments of its kind in pairs﴾. This view is more similar to the meaning of the verse in my opinion.

It has been narrated from Muqatil ibn Hayyan concerning this:

Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Rahim al-Barqi narrated to me, saying: ʿAmr ibn Abi Salama narrated to us, saying: I asked Abu Muʿadh al-Khurasani about God's saying: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾, and he informed us from Muqatil ibn Hayyan, who said: "It is abrogated (mansukha); it was abrogated by ﴿So We will not increase you except in punishment﴾." There is no meaning to this statement, because His saying: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾ is a report, and reports do not admit abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later revelation); abrogation occurs only in commands and prohibitions.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿They will not taste therein any coolness or drink﴾

He says: They will not taste therein any coolness (bard) that cools the heat of the blaze from them, except the dark, cold liquid (ghassaq), nor any drink that quenches them from the intensity of the thirst that is upon them, except scalding water (ḥamīm). Some people of knowledge of the Arabic language have claimed that bard in this place means sleep, and that the meaning of the statement is: They will not taste therein sleep or drink, citing as evidence for this view the saying of al-Kindi:

"Its sips cooled upon me, and the coolness kept me from it, and from its kisses (qublāt), the coolness."

(The report is cited by Ibn Kathir in his Tafsir (1:41–42) from this place, and al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (1:9), attributing it to al-Tabari alone. ʿAwf, who narrated from al-Hasan, is ʿAwf ibn Abi Jamila al-Abdi, known as Ibn al-Aʿrabi, and he is trustworthy and reliable.)

By bard they mean drowsiness (nuʿas), and sleep, if it cools the thirst's burning, then it is said that for this reason it is called bard, though it is not its known name. The interpretation of God's Book is according to the most common usage of the Arabic language, not otherwise.

The exegetes have said the same as what we have said about this.

Mention of those who said that:

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Abu Jaʿfar, from al-Rabiʿ: ﴿They will not taste therein any coolness or drink, except scalding water and dark, cold liquid﴾. He made an exception of scalding water from drink and of dark, cold liquid from coolness.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿except scalding water and dark, cold liquid﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: They will not taste therein any coolness or drink, except scalding water that has been heated until its heat reaches its extreme, so it is like molten metal (muhl) that scorches the faces, and no coolness except dark, cold liquid.

The exegetes differed on the meaning of ghassaq. Some of them said: It is what flows from the pus of the people of Hell.

Mention of those who said that:

Abu Kurayb and Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, both saying: Ibn Idris narrated to us, from his father, from ʿAtiyya ibn Saʿd, regarding His saying: ﴿scalding water and ghassaq﴾, he said: "It is what flows from their skins."

Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿla narrated to us, saying: al-Muʿtamir narrated to us, from his father, who said: Abu ʿAmr narrated to us, who said: ʿIkrima claimed that he had told them, regarding His saying: ﴿and ghassaq﴾, he said: "What comes out of their eyes of pus and blood."

Ibn Bashshar and Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, both saying: ʿAbd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Mansur, from Ibrahim and Abu Razin, regarding ﴿scalding water and ghassaq﴾: both said: "The washings of the people of the Fire." That is the wording of Ibn Bashshar; as for Ibn al-Muthanna, he said in his narration: "What flows from their pus."

Ibn Bashshar narrated to us again, from ʿAbd al-Rahman, saying the same as Ibn al-Muthanna.

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Mansur, from Abu Razin: ﴿and ghassaq﴾, he said: "What flows from their pus."

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Mansur and Abu Razin, from Ibrahim, the same.

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His saying: ﴿ghassaq﴾: "We used to be told that the ghassaq is what flows from between its skin and flesh."

Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: al-Dahhak ibn Makhlad narrated to us, from Sufyan, who said: "It has reached me that it is what flows from their tears."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Mansur, from Ibrahim: ﴿and ghassaq﴾, he said: "What flows from their pus from the cold." Sufyan said this, and someone else said: "The tears."

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: ﴿except scalding water and ghassaq﴾: "The hamim is the tears of their eyes in the Fire, gathered in the trenches of the Fire, and they are given to drink from it. And the ghassaq is the pus that comes out of their skins, what the Fire melts them with, in basins where it is gathered, and they are given to drink from it."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Mansur, from Ibrahim: ﴿except scalding water and ghassaq﴾, he said: "The ghassaq is what drips from their skins and what flows from their stench."

Others said: The ghassaq is the zamharir (extreme cold).

Mention of those who said that:

Ali narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Muʿawiya narrated to me, from ʿAli, from Ibn ʿAbbas: ﴿except scalding water and ghassaq﴾, he says: "The zamharir."

Abu Kurayb, Abu al-Sa'ib and Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Ibn Idris narrated to us, saying: I heard Layth, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿except scalding water and ghassaq﴾: "That which they cannot bear to taste because of its coldness."

He said: Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Layth, from Mujahid: ﴿except scalding water and ghassaq﴾, he said: "That which they cannot endure because of its cold."

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Layth, from Mujahid: "The ghassaq is that which cannot be endured because of its cold."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Abu Jaʿfar, from al-Rabiʿ, who said: "The ghassaq is the zamharir."

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Abu Jaʿfar, from al-Rabiʿ, from Abu al-ʿAliya, who said: "The ghassaq is the zamharir."

Others said: It is the stinking, and it is in al-Takhariyya (a region).

Mention of those who said that:

It was reported to me from al-Musayyab ibn Sharik, from Salih ibn Hayyan, from Abd Allah ibn Buraida, who said: "The ghassaq, in al-Takhariyya, is the stinking."

In my view, ghassaq is the fa'al pattern, from their saying: "The eye of so-and-so ghasaqat" when its tears flowed, and "the wound ghasaqa" when its pus flowed. From it is God's saying: ﴿and from the evil of the darkening (ghasiq) when it settles﴾, where by ghasiq is meant the night when it covers things and envelops them; what is intended thereby is its onslaught upon things, like the onslaught of a flowing flood. So if ghassaq is what I have described as a flowing thing, then it must be said: What God promised these people, and informed that they would taste in the Hereafter of drink, is the liquid flowing from the zamharir in Hell, which combines with its intense cold a stench.

As:

Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Yaʿmur ibn Bishr narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak narrated to us, saying: Rushdin ibn Saʿd narrated to us, saying: ʿAmr ibn al-Harith narrated to us, from Abu al-Samh, from Abu al-Haytham, from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "If a bucket of ghassaq were poured out into this world, it would make the people of this world stink."

I was told from Muhammad ibn Harb, who said: Ibn Lahi'a narrated to us, from Abu Qabil, from Abu Malik, from Abd Allah ibn ʿAmr, who said: "Do you know what the ghassaq is?" They said: "God knows best." He said: "It is thick pus. If a drop of it were poured out in the West, it would make the people of the East stink, and if it were poured out in the East, it would make the people of the West stink."

If someone says: You have said that the ghassaq is the zamharir, and the zamharir is extreme cold; so how can the zamharir be flowing? It is said: The cold that cannot be endured or borne takes on the attribute of a flowing thing from the bodies of those people, from pus and purulence.

The commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 78, verses 21–25:

﴿Indeed, Hell has been ever lying in wait﴾ ﴿for the transgressors, a place of return,﴾ ﴿remaining therein for ages.﴾ ﴿They will not taste therein any coolness or drink,﴾ ﴿except scalding water and dark, cold liquid.﴾

Concerning the interpretation of His saying: ﴿Indeed, Hell has been ever lying in wait﴾

By His saying, may His remembrance be exalted, He means: Indeed, Hell has been a place of watching for its people, those who used to deny in the world both it and the return to God in the Hereafter, and also for others among those who affirm it. The meaning of the statement is: Indeed, Hell has been a place of lying in wait, watching for whoever passes through it and keeping an eye on them.

The exegetes (ahl al-ta'wil) have said the same as what we have said about this.

Mention of those who said that:

Zakariyya ibn Yahya ibn Abi Za'ida narrated to us, saying: Muslim ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, from Abd Allah ibn Bakr ibn Abd Allah al-Muzani, who said: Al-Hasan, whenever he recited this verse, ﴿Indeed, Hell has been ever lying in wait﴾, would say: "Indeed, at the gate there is a watchman. Whoever comes with a pass will pass through, and whoever does not come with a pass will be detained."

Ya'qub narrated to me, saying: Isma'il ibn Ulayya narrated to us, from Abu Raja', from al-Hasan, regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, Hell has been ever lying in wait﴾, he said: "No one enters Paradise until he passes through the Fire."

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, Hell has been ever lying in wait﴾, he said: "It informs us that there is no path to Paradise until one crosses the Fire."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan: ﴿Indeed, Hell has been ever lying in wait﴾, he said: "On it are three bridges."

* *

As for His saying: ﴿for the transgressors, a place of return﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Indeed, Hell is, for those who transgressed in the world, who exceeded the limits of God out of arrogance toward their Lord, a dwelling and a place of return, to which they return, and a destination to which they go, to dwell in it.

The exegetes have said the same as what we have said about this.

Mention of those who said that:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada: ﴿a place of return﴾, meaning a dwelling and a refuge.

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan: ﴿a place of return﴾, he said: "A place of return and a dwelling."

* *

As for His saying: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Indeed, these transgressors in the world will remain in Hell, abiding therein for ages.

The readers (qurra') differed in the recitation of His saying: ﴿labithin﴾. The majority of the readers of Medina and Basra, and some readers of Kufa, recited it as ﴿labithin﴾ with an alif (lābithīn). The majority of the readers of Kufa recited it as "labithin" without an alif (labithīn). The more eloquent of the two readings, and the one more sound in its grammatical derivation in Arabic, is the reading of the one who recites it with the alif. This is because the Arabs hardly ever use an adjective of the pattern fa'il (ʿafila) and then make it govern something and put it in the accusative by it. They would not say: "This is a man stingy (bakhil) with his wealth," nor "it was difficult (asir) for us," nor "he is a quarrelsome opponent (khasim) to us," because such a pattern as fa'ila does not come as an adjective except to praise or blame, so the praise or blame does not govern anything other than itself. When they want to make such a word govern a noun or something else, they make it an active participle (fā'il) and say: "He is bakhil with his wealth" (bākhil bi-mālihi), and "he is ṭāmi' in what is with us" (ṭāmi' fīmā 'indanā). Therefore I said that lābithīn is more sound in its grammatical derivation in Arabic and more eloquent. I have not deemed lawful the reading of the one who recites labithin, although the other is more eloquent, because the Arabs sometimes make praise govern nouns. A verse of Labid is recited:

"Or a mislah ʿamil, a flank of a smooth-skinned she-ass (samaḥj), with its shoulders having wounds and sores."

So ʿamil governed ʿiḍāda (flank), and if it were an active participle it would have been more eloquent. It is also recited:

"... ... ... ... ... ... ... ... ... and with the axe, a striker of the heads of the karanif (thistle/hard-headed)."

And from it is the saying of ʿAbbās ibn Mirdas:

"More fearless and more protective of the truth than them, and striking with swords the helmets (qawānis) more than us."

As for al-aḥqāb (ages), it is the plural of ḥuqb, and ḥiqab is the plural of ḥiqba, as the poet said:

"We lived like the two companions of Jadhima for an age (ḥiqba) of time, until it was said: we shall not separate."

So this is plural ḥiqab, and among the uses of aḥqāb whose plural is ḥuqb is God's saying: ﴿or I will continue for a long age (ḥuqb)﴾. So this is the singular of aḥqāb.

The exegetes differed concerning the duration of a ḥuqb. Some of them said: it is a duration of three hundred years.

Mention of those who said that:

ʿImran ibn Musa al-Qazzaz narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Warith ibn Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Ishaq ibn Suwayd narrated to us, from Bashir ibn Ka'b, regarding His saying: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾, he said: "It has reached me that a ḥuqb is three hundred years, each year three hundred and sixty days, each day a thousand years."

Others said: rather, the duration of one ḥuqb is eighty years.

Mention of those who said that:

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, who said: ʿAmmar al-Duhni narrated to me, from Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd, who said: ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, said to Hilal al-Hajari: "What do you find of the ḥuqb in the revealed Book of God?" He said: "We find eighty years, each year twelve months, each month thirty days, each day a thousand years."

Tamim ibn al-Muntasir narrated to us, saying: Ishaq informed us, from Shurayk, from ʿAsim ibn Abi al-Najud, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayra, that he said: "The ḥuqb is eighty years, the year is three hundred and sixty days, and the day is a thousand years."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Abu Sinan, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The ḥuqb is eighty years."

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Jabir ibn Nuh narrated to us, saying: al-Aʿmash narrated to us, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, regarding His saying: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾, he said: "The ḥuqb is eighty years, the year is three hundred and sixty days, the day is a year or a thousand years" [al-Tabari is doubtful].

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatada, who said: God said: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾, and it is that which has no end; whenever one ḥuqb passes, another ḥuqb comes after it. It was mentioned to us that the ḥuqb is eighty years.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿla narrated to us, saying: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Maʿmar, from Qatada, regarding His saying: ﴿aḥqāban﴾, he said: "It has reached us that the ḥuqb is eighty years of the years of the Hereafter."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Abu Jaʿfar, from al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾, "No one knows the number of these ages except God, but one ḥuqb is eighty years, the year is three hundred and sixty days, and each day of that is a thousand years."

Others said: One ḥuqb is seventy thousand years.

Mention of those who said that:

Ibn ʿAbd al-Rahim al-Barqi narrated to me, saying: ʿAmr ibn Abi Salama narrated to me, from Zuhayr, from Salim, who said: I heard al-Hasan being asked about God's saying: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾, and he said: "As for the ages, there is no count of them except eternity in the Fire; but they mentioned that one ḥuqb is seventy thousand years, each day of those seventy thousand days being like a thousand years of what you count."

ʿAmr ibn ʿAbd al-Hamid al-Amuli narrated to us, saying: Abu Usama narrated to us, from Hisham, from al-Hasan, regarding His saying: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾, he said: "As for the ages, no one knows what they are, but one ḥuqb is seventy thousand years, each day like a thousand years."

It is narrated from Khalid ibn Maʿdan regarding this verse that it refers to the people of the qibla (Muslims).

Mention of those who said that:

ʿAli narrated to us, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Muʿawiya ibn Salih narrated to me, from ʿAmir ibn Jashb, from Khalid ibn Maʿdan, regarding His saying: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾, and His saying: ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, that both refer to the people of monotheism from among the people of the qibla.

If someone says: What do you say about this report? It is said: What Qatada said from al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas about this is more sound. If he says: "Then for the disbelievers there is no punishment except ages," it is said: Indeed al-Rabiʿ and Qatada both said that these ages have no end and no cessation. It may also be that the meaning of it is: remaining therein for ages in this type of punishment, and that they: ﴿will not taste therein any coolness or drink, except scalding water and dark, cold liquid﴾. Then when those ages are over, they will have other kinds of punishment beyond that, as God, may His praise be exalted, said in His Book: ﴿And indeed for the transgressors is an evil place of return: Hell, which they will burn in, and wretched is the resting place. This—so let them taste it: scalding water and dark, cold liquid, and other punishments of its kind in pairs﴾. This view is more similar to the meaning of the verse in my opinion.

It has been narrated from Muqatil ibn Hayyan concerning this:

Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Rahim al-Barqi narrated to me, saying: ʿAmr ibn Abi Salama narrated to us, saying: I asked Abu Muʿadh al-Khurasani about God's saying: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾, and he informed us from Muqatil ibn Hayyan, who said: "It is abrogated (mansukha); it was abrogated by ﴿So We will not increase you except in punishment﴾." There is no meaning to this statement, because His saying: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾ is a report, and reports do not admit abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later revelation); abrogation occurs only in commands and prohibitions.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿They will not taste therein any coolness or drink﴾

He says: They will not taste therein any coolness (bard) that cools the heat of the blaze from them, except the dark, cold liquid (ghassaq), nor any drink that quenches them from the intensity of the thirst that is upon them, except scalding water (ḥamīm). Some people of knowledge of the Arabic language have claimed that bard in this place means sleep, and that the meaning of the statement is: They will not taste therein sleep or drink, citing as evidence for this view the saying of al-Kindi:

"Its sips cooled upon me, and the coolness kept me from it, and from its kisses (qublāt), the coolness."

(The report is cited by Ibn Kathir in his Tafsir (1:41–42) from this place, and al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (1:9), attributing it to al-Tabari alone. ʿAwf, who narrated from al-Hasan, is ʿAwf ibn Abi Jamila al-Abdi, known as Ibn al-Aʿrabi, and he is trustworthy and reliable.)

By bard they mean drowsiness (nuʿas), and sleep, if it cools the thirst's burning, then it is said that for this reason it is called bard, though it is not its known name. The interpretation of God's Book is according to the most common usage of the Arabic language, not otherwise.

The exegetes have said the same as what we have said about this.

Mention of those who said that:

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Abu Jaʿfar, from al-Rabiʿ: ﴿They will not taste therein any coolness or drink, except scalding water and dark, cold liquid﴾. He made an exception of scalding water from drink and of dark, cold liquid from coolness.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿except scalding water and dark, cold liquid﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: They will not taste therein any coolness or drink, except scalding water that has been heated until its heat reaches its extreme, so it is like molten metal (muhl) that scorches the faces, and no coolness except dark, cold liquid.

The exegetes differed on the meaning of ghassaq. Some of them said: It is what flows from the pus of the people of Hell.

Mention of those who said that:

Abu Kurayb and Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, both saying: Ibn Idris narrated to us, from his father, from ʿAtiyya ibn Saʿd, regarding His saying: ﴿scalding water and ghassaq﴾, he said: "It is what flows from their skins."

Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿla narrated to us, saying: al-Muʿtamir narrated to us, from his father, who said: Abu ʿAmr narrated to us, who said: ʿIkrima claimed that he had told them, regarding His saying: ﴿and ghassaq﴾, he said: "What comes out of their eyes of pus and blood."

Ibn Bashshar and Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, both saying: ʿAbd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Mansur, from Ibrahim and Abu Razin, regarding ﴿scalding water and ghassaq﴾: both said: "The washings of the people of the Fire." That is the wording of Ibn Bashshar; as for Ibn al-Muthanna, he said in his narration: "What flows from their pus."

Ibn Bashshar narrated to us again, from ʿAbd al-Rahman, saying the same as Ibn al-Muthanna.

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Mansur, from Abu Razin: ﴿and ghassaq﴾, he said: "What flows from their pus."

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Mansur and Abu Razin, from Ibrahim, the same.

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His saying: ﴿ghassaq﴾: "We used to be told that the ghassaq is what flows from between its skin and flesh."

Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: al-Dahhak ibn Makhlad narrated to us, from Sufyan, who said: "It has reached me that it is what flows from their tears."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Mansur, from Ibrahim: ﴿and ghassaq﴾, he said: "What flows from their pus from the cold." Sufyan said this, and someone else said: "The tears."

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: ﴿except scalding water and ghassaq﴾: "The hamim is the tears of their eyes in the Fire, gathered in the trenches of the Fire, and they are given to drink from it. And the ghassaq is the pus that comes out of their skins, what the Fire melts them with, in basins where it is gathered, and they are given to drink from it."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Mansur, from Ibrahim: ﴿except scalding water and ghassaq﴾, he said: "The ghassaq is what drips from their skins and what flows from their stench."

Others said: The ghassaq is the zamharir (extreme cold).

Mention of those who said that:

Ali narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Muʿawiya narrated to me, from ʿAli, from Ibn ʿAbbas: ﴿except scalding water and ghassaq﴾, he says: "The zamharir."

Abu Kurayb, Abu al-Sa'ib and Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Ibn Idris narrated to us, saying: I heard Layth, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿except scalding water and ghassaq﴾: "That which they cannot bear to taste because of its coldness."

He said: Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Layth, from Mujahid: ﴿except scalding water and ghassaq﴾, he said: "That which they cannot endure because of its cold."

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Layth, from Mujahid: "The ghassaq is that which cannot be endured because of its cold."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Mihran narrated to us, from Abu Jaʿfar, from al-Rabiʿ, who said: "The ghassaq is the zamharir."

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Abu Jaʿfar, from al-Rabiʿ, from Abu al-ʿAliya, who said: "The ghassaq is the zamharir."

Others said: It is the stinking, and it is in al-Takhariyya (a region).

Mention of those who said that:

It was reported to me from al-Musayyab ibn Sharik, from Salih ibn Hayyan, from Abd Allah ibn Buraida, who said: "The ghassaq, in al-Takhariyya, is the stinking."

In my view, ghassaq is the fa'al pattern, from their saying: "The eye of so-and-so ghasaqat" when its tears flowed, and "the wound ghasaqa" when its pus flowed. From it is God's saying: ﴿and from the evil of the darkening (ghasiq) when it settles﴾, where by ghasiq is meant the night when it covers things and envelops them; what is intended thereby is its onslaught upon things, like the onslaught of a flowing flood. So if ghassaq is what I have described as a flowing thing, then it must be said: What God promised these people, and informed that they would taste in the Hereafter of drink, is the liquid flowing from the zamharir in Hell, which combines with its intense cold a stench.
